## D1 · Label it

Prepares Guided Project [task 1](guided-project.qmd#task-1){target="_blank"} (A1, B1).

**Goal.** A reader should understand the plot without you there: a title that
says what it shows, a subtitle with the data and its n (sample size: the number of penguins
in each group), axis titles with units, a legend title, and percent labels for a share. (Session 1.)

**Your turn.** Label the share of Adelie penguins on each island.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island, fill = species == "Adelie")) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "___",
    subtitle = "___",
    x = "___",
    y = "___",
    fill = "___"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = ___)
```
:::


**Investigate.** Which label would a reader miss most if you left it out?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island, fill = species == "Adelie")) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Torgersen's penguins are all Adelie",
    subtitle = "Palmer penguins, 344 penguins on three islands",
    x = "Share of the island's penguins (%)",
    y = "Island",
    fill = "Adelie"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-alt='Sideways stacked bar chart of the share of Adelie penguins on each island, labeled in percent, where Torgersen is 100% Adelie, Dream about 45% and Biscoe about 26%.' width=672}
:::
:::


The title states the finding; the subtitle says which data and how many; the
x-axis says "share of what" and its unit. Torgersen is 100% Adelie (52 of
52), Dream about 45% (56 of 124), Biscoe about 26% (44 of 168).
:::

## D2 · Choose a scale

Prepares Guided Project [task 2](guided-project.qmd#task-2){target="_blank"} (A2, B2).

**Goal.** Which scale fits the data? (Session 1.)

**Your turn.** Plot life expectancy against GDP per person in 2007, first on
a linear x-axis, then on a log x-axis.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gap_2007 <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007)

p_wealth <- ggplot(gap_2007, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "GDP per person (US$)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")

p_wealth
p_wealth + ___(labels = scales::comma)
```
:::


**Investigate.** Where are most countries on the linear axis? What does the
log axis show that the linear one hides?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
gap_2007 <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007)

p_wealth <- ggplot(gap_2007, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "GDP per person (US$)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")

p_wealth
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-alt='Scatter plot of life expectancy against GDP per person in 2007 on a linear x-axis, where most countries are crowded at the left below 10,000 dollars and a few rich countries spread to the right.' width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
p_wealth +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "GDP per person (US$, log scale)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-2.png){fig-alt='The same scatter plot with a log x-axis, where the countries spread evenly and life expectancy rises steadily with each tenfold step in GDP per person.' width=672}
:::
:::


GDP per person runs from about \$278 to \$49,357 across 142 countries, and
66 of them are below \$5,000: on a linear axis they crowd into the left
edge. On a log axis each step is ten times the one before, so the poorer
countries spread out and the pattern (life expectancy rises with each
tenfold step) shows. Say "log scale" in the axis title: a reader who misses
it reads the gaps wrong.
:::

## D3 · The Lie Factor

Prepares Guided Project [task 2](guided-project.qmd#task-2){target="_blank"}: a scale is honest only if sizes in the
picture match the data.

The **Lie Factor** (Tufte, 2001, p. 57) compares the size of an effect in the
picture with its size in the data: drawn ratio ÷ data ratio. 1 is honest;
above 1 exaggerates; below 1 understates.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lie_factors <- tibble(
  case = c("Module 12: penguin bars zoomed to start at 40",
           "Minard's march, default line widths (1 to 6)",
           "Minard's march, range = c(0.1, 8.5)"),
  drawn_ratio = c((168 - 40) / (52 - 40), 6 / 1, 8.5 / 0.1),
  data_ratio = c(168 / 52, 340000 / 4000, 340000 / 4000)
) %>%
  mutate(lie_factor = drawn_ratio / data_ratio)

lie_factors
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  case                                         drawn_ratio data_ratio lie_factor
  <chr>                                              <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Module 12: penguin bars zoomed to start at …        10.7       3.23     3.30  
2 Minard's march, default line widths (1 to 6)         6        85        0.0706
3 Minard's march, range = c(0.1, 8.5)                 85        85        1     
```


:::
:::


**Talk.** Which case exaggerates, which understates, and which is honest?
Why does the default width scale understate Minard's losses so much?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

- **Bars cut at 40, about 3.3: exaggerates.** Biscoe (168) looks about 10.7
  times as long as Torgersen (52), but the counts differ only 3.2 times.
- **Minard, default widths, about 0.07: understates.** The army shrinks from
  340,000 to 4,000 (85 times), but `scale_linewidth()` draws widths from 1 to
  6 by default: only 6 times. (In class you measured them with
  `layer_data()`.)
- **Minard, `range = c(0.1, 8.5)`, 1: honest.** 8.5 ÷ 0.1 = 85, the same
  ratio as the data.
:::

## D4 · Fixed or free panels

Prepares Guided Project [task 3](guided-project.qmd#task-3){target="_blank"} (A3, B3).

**Goal.** One plot or many? And when the panels differ in size, fixed or
free axes? (Session 2.)

**Your turn.** Plot each continent's total population over time, one panel
per continent. Then free the y-axis.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pop_by_continent <- gapminder %>%
  group_by(continent, year) %>%
  summarize(pop_millions = sum(pop) / 1e6, .groups = "drop")

p_pop <- ggplot(pop_by_continent, aes(x = year, y = pop_millions)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Population (millions)")

p_pop + facet_wrap(vars(___))
p_pop + facet_wrap(vars(___), scales = "___")
```
:::


**Investigate.** On the fixed panels, what happened to Oceania between 1952
and 2007? On the free panels? Which version would mislead a reader, and how?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
pop_by_continent <- gapminder %>%
  group_by(continent, year) %>%
  summarize(pop_millions = sum(pop) / 1e6, .groups = "drop")

p_pop <- ggplot(pop_by_continent, aes(x = year, y = pop_millions)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Population (millions)")

p_pop + facet_wrap(vars(continent))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-alt='Five panels of total population over time by continent on one shared y-axis, where Asia rises steeply to about 3,800 million and Oceania looks like a flat line near zero.' width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
p_pop + facet_wrap(vars(continent), scales = "free_y")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-2.png){fig-alt='The same five panels with free y-axes, where every continent shows a rising line, including Oceania, whose axis only reaches about 25 million.' width=672}
:::
:::


Fixed axes compare sizes: Asia grows from about 1,395 to 3,812 million, and
Oceania (2 countries, 10.7 to 24.5 million) looks flat. Free axes compare
shapes: Oceania more than doubles, like the others. Each is honest only if
the reader notices the axes: with free y, say so in the caption, because
panels of equal height no longer mean equal numbers.
:::

## D5 · Two facets at once: sex and species

Prepares Guided Project [task 3](guided-project.qmd#task-3){target="_blank"}: panels by two columns, and the n of what
is left out.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins %>%
  drop_na(sex, body_mass_g) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 200) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(sex), cols = vars(species)) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Penguins")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-alt='Grid of histograms of penguin body mass, rows for female and male, columns for Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo, where males are heavier than females within every species and Gentoo are the heaviest.' width=672}
:::
:::


**Talk.** What can you compare across a row? Down a column? 11 penguins have
no recorded sex (6 Adelie, 5 Gentoo) and are not in this plot: where would
you tell the reader?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

Across a row: the three species, for one sex (Gentoo are the heaviest).
Down a column: females and males of one species (males are heavier in each).
The shared axes make both comparisons fair. Say the 11 missing penguins in
the caption or the text, with their n.
:::

## D6 · Uncertainty clouds

Prepares Guided Project [task 4](guided-project.qmd#task-4){target="_blank"} (A4, B4).

**Goal.** Is a difference between two groups large or small? Compared to
what? Put each penguin next to the means of 200 resampled samples, on the
same axis. (Session 2.)

**Your turn.** Compare Adelie and Chinstrap flipper lengths. The prepared
code draws each species' penguins again (with replacement, the same number),
200 times, and keeps each sample's mean. Then make one panel per `kind`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(3901)
flippers <- penguins %>%
  filter(species %in% c("Adelie", "Chinstrap")) %>%
  drop_na(flipper_length_mm) %>%
  select(species, flipper_length_mm)

means <- map(1:200, function(i) {
  flippers %>%
    group_by(species) %>%
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE) %>%
    summarize(flipper_length_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm))
}) %>%
  bind_rows()

clouds <- bind_rows(
  flippers %>% mutate(kind = "Individual penguins"),
  means %>% mutate(kind = "Resampled means")
)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(clouds, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ ___) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```
:::


**Investigate.** In which panel do the two clouds overlap? What does that
say about two penguins, and about the two means?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(clouds, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ kind) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-alt='Two panels on one shared y-axis: on the left, every Adelie and Chinstrap penguin\'s flipper length, two tall clouds that overlap almost completely; on the right, 200 resampled means per species, two short clouds about 6 mm apart that don\'t overlap.' width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
clouds %>%
  group_by(kind, species) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), mean = mean(flipper_length_mm),
            lowest = min(flipper_length_mm),
            highest = max(flipper_length_mm), .groups = "drop")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  kind                species       n  mean lowest highest
  <chr>               <fct>     <int> <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Individual penguins Adelie      151  190.   172     210 
2 Individual penguins Chinstrap    68  196.   178     212 
3 Resampled means     Adelie      200  190.   189.    191.
4 Resampled means     Chinstrap   200  196.   194.    198.
```


:::
:::


In the left panel the clouds overlap almost completely: Adelie flippers run
from 172 to 210 mm, Chinstrap from 178 to 212 mm, so many Adelie penguins
have longer flippers than many Chinstrap ones. In the right panel the 200
resampled means don't overlap: Adelie's from 188.7 to 191.3 mm, Chinstrap's
from 193.6 to 197.8 mm. The gap between the means, 5.9 mm (189.95 and
195.82), is small next to the spread of the penguins (sd 6.5 and 7.1 mm) but
large next to how far each mean moves from sample to sample. Say which you
compare: individuals or means. Chinstrap's cloud of means is wider: 68
penguins, against Adelie's 151.

In the Guided Project, `make_clouds()` does the resampling for you.
:::

### Watch the means settle

Draw 200 samples of 10, of 50, and of each species' full size (with
replacement), and plot each sample's mean flipper length.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(3901)
flippers <- drop_na(penguins, flipper_length_mm)

cloud <- map_dfr(c(10, 50, NA), function(size) {
  map_dfr(1:200, function(i) {
    grouped <- group_by(flippers, species)
    drawn <- if (is.na(size)) {
      slice_sample(grouped, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)   # each species' n
    } else {
      slice_sample(grouped, n = size, replace = TRUE)
    }
    drawn %>%
      summarize(mean_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm), .groups = "drop") %>%
      mutate(sample = if (is.na(size)) "All penguins" else
               paste(size, "penguins"))
  })
}) %>%
  mutate(sample = fct_inorder(sample))

ggplot(cloud, aes(x = mean_mm, y = species)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(vars(sample), ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean flipper length of one sample (mm)", y = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-alt='Three panels of dots, one per resampled mean flipper length for each species, for samples of 10, 50 and all penguins; the clouds of means are wide for 10 and narrow steadily as the sample grows, and the three species separate more clearly.' width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
cloud %>%
  group_by(sample, species) %>%
  summarize(spread_sd = sd(mean_mm), .groups = "drop")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 9 × 3
  sample       species   spread_sd
  <fct>        <fct>         <dbl>
1 10 penguins  Adelie        2.10 
2 10 penguins  Chinstrap     2.14 
3 10 penguins  Gentoo        2.09 
4 50 penguins  Adelie        0.932
5 50 penguins  Chinstrap     0.932
6 50 penguins  Gentoo        0.908
7 All penguins Adelie        0.520
8 All penguins Chinstrap     0.824
9 All penguins Gentoo        0.612
```


:::
:::


The bigger the sample, the less its mean moves from one sample to the next.
For Adelie, the spread (sd) of the 200 means is about 2.1 mm with 10
penguins, 0.93 mm with 50, and 0.52 mm with all 151. In one sentence, the
central limit theorem: means of larger samples pile up in a narrower,
bell-shaped cloud around the true mean, and the cloud's width shrinks with
the square root of the sample size. So "compared to what?" matters: a
difference between two means is big or small compared to that width (the
se), not to the spread of the penguins themselves (the sd).

## D7 · Color for every reader

Prepares Guided Project [task 5](guided-project.qmd#task-5){target="_blank"} (A5, B5).

**Goal.** Colors every reader can tell apart, and never color alone.
(Session 1.)


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
species_labels <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(flipper_length_mm, bill_length_mm) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(flipper_length_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm),
            bill_length_mm = max(bill_length_mm))

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm,
                     color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_label(data = species_labels, aes(label = species)) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Bill length (mm)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-alt='Scatter plot of bill length against flipper length for the three penguin species in three viridis colors, each species labeled directly next to its cloud of points.' width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "GDP per person (US$, log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)", color = "Continent")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-2.png){fig-alt='Scatter plot of life expectancy against GDP per person in 2007 on a log axis, with the five continents in five viridis colors that are hard to tell apart.' width=672}
:::
:::


**What the numbers mean.** We simulate how the colors look to readers with
three types of color blindness, then measure how far apart the two closest
colors are (a standard color difference, delta E). Bigger is easier to tell
apart; 20 is our course's line for clearly different. The red-green
simulations come from a validated model; the blue-yellow one is an
approximation. (In the Guided Project, `color_check()` makes this table for
your plot, and `simulate_plot()` redraws your plot in the simulated
colors.)


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


Table: Smallest difference between any two colors.

|view                      | 3 species| 5 continents|
|:-------------------------|---------:|------------:|
|Red-green (deuteranopia)  |      30.5|         17.5|
|Red-green (protanopia)    |      41.1|         19.7|
|Blue-yellow (approximate) |      29.7|         17.2|


:::
:::


**Talk.** Which plot passes the course rule (at least 20 in all three rows)?
What could carry the continents instead of color alone?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

Three species pass (30.5, 41.1 and 29.7); five continents fail (17.5, 19.7
and 17.2): with more groups the colors have less room. The penguin plot
also names each species on the plot, so color is never the only cue. For the
continents: panels (`facet_wrap(vars(continent))`, D4), direct labels, or
fewer groups, combined with care and said in the caption.
:::

**Where the numbers come from.** The simulations use the model of Machado,
Oliveira and Fernandes (2009), at full severity. The red-green simulations
come from a validated model; the blue-yellow one is an approximation.

Machado, G. M., Oliveira, M. M., & Fernandes, L. A. F. (2009). A
physiologically-based model for simulation of color vision deficiency.
*IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 15*(6),
1291–1298. <https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2009.113>

## D8 · Check a deck

Prepares Guided Project [task 6](guided-project.qmd#task-6){target="_blank"} (your slides).

**Goal.** Check a finished deck against the minimum elements. (Session 2.)

**Your turn.** Open the penguins slides in the **Example** menu of your own
site (or the [course example](https://acintron-cc.github.io/cis-3901-202710/example/penguins_slides.html)).
Find each element: title; question (naming the groups compared); data (source,
what one row is, how many rows); figure; what it shows (a headline that
states the finding); limitations; sources and AI use.

**Investigate.** Which elements share a slide? Which one is missing, and does
your deck need it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

The question is the title ("Do penguin species differ in flipper length?").
The headline slide states the finding in its heading, with the figure under
it. The last slide holds what it shows, the limitations (344 penguins, three

## D9 · More scale choices: size, gray fills, redundant cues

Prepares Guided Project [task 5](guided-project.qmd#task-5){target="_blank"} (a second cue besides color) and
[task 2](guided-project.qmd#task-2){target="_blank"} (honest sizes).

### Size: area or radius?


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
p_size <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "GDP per person (US$, log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)", size = "Population")

p_size + scale_size_area(max_size = 12, labels = scales::comma)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-alt='Scatter plot of 2007 life expectancy against GDP per person with points sized by population using scale_size_area, so a country\'s circle area is proportional to its population and China and India dominate.' width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
p_size + scale_radius(range = c(1, 12), labels = scales::comma)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-2.png){fig-alt='The same plot with scale_radius, where the circle radius is proportional to population, so the largest countries look far bigger and small countries nearly vanish.' width=672}
:::
:::


Readers judge circles by their area. With `scale_size_area()` area is
proportional to population, so a country twice as large has twice the ink.
With `scale_radius()` the radius is proportional, so the area grows with the
square: big countries are exaggerated (a Lie Factor above 1).

### Gray fills, no optical art


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_grey(start = 0.25, end = 0.75) +
  labs(x = "Penguins", y = "Island", fill = "Species")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-alt='Stacked bar chart of penguin counts per island split by species in three shades of gray from dark to light, with no hatching or patterns.' width=672}
:::
:::


Hatching and stripes can shimmer on screen (Tufte's "optical art"). Plain gray
shades print well and never vibrate; keep them few, and far enough apart.

### One redundant cue


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm,
                     color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Bill length (mm)",
       color = "Species", shape = "Species")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](practice_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-alt='Scatter plot of bill length against flipper length where each species has both its own viridis color and its own point shape: circles, triangles and squares.' width=672}
:::
:::


Mapping species to both color and shape is redundant on purpose: it helps a
reader who can't tell the colors apart, or who prints the page in gray. It
helps most with few groups and few overlapping points; with many groups,
shapes get hard to tell apart too, and panels work better.
